title: Are Trekking Poles Worth It? Buying a Pair in Nairobi for Kenya's Steep Descents
meta_title: Trekking Poles in Nairobi: Steady Knees on 600 m Descents
meta_description: How to choose trekking poles in Nairobi: folding vs telescoping, the right length for your height, using them on Longonot ash, and where to buy a pair.
excerpt: How to choose trekking poles in Nairobi for Mt Longonot's ash, Aberdare bogs and Mt Kenya scree: folding or telescoping, sizing by height, technique, care and where to buy.
content:
Halfway down the loose ash below Mt Longonot's crater rim is where many hikers start wishing they had bought trekking poles in Nairobi before the trip. A good pole takes load off your knees on descents, steadies you on mud and scree, and should fold or collapse small enough to strap to a daypack.

Poles look like an optional extra until the first steep, slippery descent of the short rains. Then they become the piece of kit everyone wants to borrow. Below we cover where trekking poles in Nairobi earn their place on Kenyan trails, folding versus telescoping designs, how to set the right length for your height, what to check before you pay, how to use them properly, and where to buy a pair in the city.

Quick Facts

  • Knee load: a 1999 study in the Journal of Sports Sciences measured 12-25% lower knee joint forces when walkers used poles on a steep descent.
  • Right length on flat ground: your elbow bends to about 90 degrees with the tip on the ground beside your boot.
  • On slopes: shorten each pole by roughly 5-10 cm for descents and lengthen it by the same for long climbs.
  • Two main designs: most trekking poles in Nairobi are either folding (Z-style), which pack shortest, or telescoping, which adjust over a wider range.
  • Where they help most near Nairobi: the ash descent on Mt Longonot (rim at 2,776 m), the long forest walk down Ol Donyo Sabuk and the boggy Aberdare moorland.
  • Flying: pack poles in checked luggage for flights to Kilimanjaro; most airport security treats them as hold items, so confirm with your airline.

Are Trekking Poles Worth It on Kenyan Trails?

Yes, for most hikers. Trekking poles are worth carrying on any Kenyan hike with a long or loose descent, wet ground, or a heavy pack. They matter less on short, flat forest walks, and they get in the way on hands-on scrambles.

The strongest evidence is for going downhill. A team of sports scientists found that walkers using poles on a steep downhill path put noticeably less force through the knee, with the study on knee joint forces with hiking poles reporting reductions of roughly 12-25%. Poles also add two points of contact, which is why guides on Mt Kenya and Kilimanjaro so often recommend them for the long walk down.

Descents: where poles earn their keep

On Mt Longonot, the climb from the gate at about 2,150 m to the crater rim is steep and dusty, and the way back down is worse because the volcanic ash rolls under your boots like marbles. Planting a pole ahead of each step turns a nervous shuffle into a steady walk. The same goes for the 9-10 km descent from the summit of Ol Donyo Sabuk, which our Kilimambogo route guide describes as rockiest in its final kilometres.

Higher up, the scree below Point Lenana on Mt Kenya and the long descent to Shipton's Camp at about 4,200 m are exactly the ground that most trekking poles in Nairobi are bought for. Tired legs, thin air and loose stones are a poor mix without an extra point of balance.

Mud, bogs and the short rains

From roughly October to December, the short rains turn red-soil paths into grease. A pole lets you test whether a puddle hides a hole, brace on a slippery bank, and keep your weight centred when one boot slides. On the Aberdare moorland around Table Mountain and Oldoinyo Lesatima, tussock grass and bog make every step uncertain, and a pole with a small basket stops the tip sinking out of sight. So when you compare trekking poles in Nairobi before the rains, check that baskets come with them or can be fitted.

River crossings are the other wet-season job. Two poles and two feet make a stable four-legged stance in moving water, and you can probe the depth before committing. Unclip the backpack hip belt first, so you can shed the pack if you slip. Any sturdy pair of trekking poles in Nairobi will do this job, folding or telescoping.

When to stow them

Poles become a nuisance where you need your hands. The rock steps in Hell's Gate's Ol Njorowa Gorge, some ladders and fixed-rope sections, and the scrambly final approach on a few volcanic peaks are easier with the poles collapsed and strapped to your pack. On a flat, well-made path such as the main loops in Karura Forest, most people simply do not need them. This is where trekking poles in Nairobi that fold small really pay off.

Hike near NairobiTerrain that mattersValue of poles
Mt Longonot (about 13.5 km circuit)Steep, loose ash on the climb and descentHigh, especially going down
Ol Donyo Sabuk (18-20 km return)Long, steady road and forest descent, rocky near the topHigh for knees on the way down
Table Mountain and Oldoinyo Lesatima, AberdaresBog, tussock grass, cold wet moorlandHigh, with baskets fitted

Mt Kenya to Point Lenana (4,985 m)Scree, frozen ground, long descents over several daysVery high; most trekkers carry two

Folding or Telescoping: Which Trekking Poles in Nairobi Suit You?

Among trekking poles in Nairobi, folding poles suit hikers who want the smallest pack size and travel by matatu or plane. Telescoping poles suit hikers who share poles, switch between very different terrain, or need a wide range of lengths. Both work well when the locks hold firm.

Folding (Z-style) poles

A folding pole breaks into three or four sections held together by an internal cord, a bit like a tent pole. Pull the sections together and a button or collar locks the pole at full length. Folded, many sit at around 35-40 cm, short enough to slide into the side pocket of a daypack or a carry-on bag. That makes folding trekking poles in Nairobi a good match for hikers who reach trailheads by matatu.

The trade-off is adjustment. Some folding poles have a fixed length, so you must buy the one that matches your height; others add a short adjustable top section. If you shop for folding trekking poles in Nairobi, check the length range printed on the shaft against the sizing table further down.

Telescoping poles and their locks

Telescoping trekking poles in Nairobi have two or three sections that slide inside one another. They adjust over a wide range, which makes them easy to share in a family and handy for long climbs and descents where you change the length. Locks come in two kinds:

  • Lever or flick locks: an external clamp you snap shut. Easy to check at a glance and to tighten with a small screw when it loosens.
  • Twist locks: an internal expander you tighten by turning the sections. Neat and light, but grit and wet can make them slip or seize.

For dusty Kenyan trails, lever locks are the easier choice when buying trekking poles in Nairobi, because you can see whether they are closed and fix them with a coin at the roadside.

Aluminium or carbon fibre?

Aluminium poles are heavier but tend to bend rather than snap, and a slight bend often still lets you walk out. Carbon fibre shafts are lighter and absorb more vibration, but they can crack if wedged between rocks and loaded sideways. For rough volcanic ground and the occasional rough handling on a matatu roof rack, aluminium is the safer everyday choice if you are buying trekking poles in Nairobi for regular weekend hikes. Carbon suits weight-conscious trekkers heading for Kilimanjaro who will look after their kit.

Grips, straps, tips and baskets

Grips on trekking poles in Nairobi come in cork, foam and rubber. Cork moulds to your hand and copes well with sweaty days in the Rift Valley heat. Foam is light and soft, though it wears faster. Rubber feels cold and can rub in hot weather, so it suits cooler mountain use. An extended foam section below the main grip lets you choke down on short, steep pitches without changing the length.

Most tips on trekking poles in Nairobi are hard carbide, which grips rock and packed earth. Rubber tip covers quieten the pole and protect it on tarmac or bare rock, and they are kinder to worn, eroded paths. Small trekking baskets stop the tip sinking into mud and bog; big snow baskets are rarely needed in Kenya.

How Long Should a Trekking Pole Be for Your Height?

A trekking pole is the right length when your elbow bends to about 90 degrees with the tip on flat ground beside your boot. As a starting point, multiply your height by roughly 0.68, then fine-tune on the trail. The same rule works for all trekking poles in Nairobi, folding or telescoping.

Your heightStarting pole length (flat ground)Long descent
150-155 cmAbout 100-105 cmAbout 95-100 cm
156-165 cmAbout 105-110 cmAbout 100-105 cm
166-175 cmAbout 115-120 cmAbout 105-110 cm
176-185 cmAbout 120-125 cmAbout 115-120 cm
186 cm and overAbout 130 cmAbout 120-125 cm

Changing the length on the hill

Going up, a slightly shorter pole lets you plant it beside your front foot and push. On a long climb many hikers shorten it by 5-10 cm; on a long traverse, shorten the uphill pole and lengthen the downhill one. Going down, lengthen the poles by about 5-10 cm so you can reach the ground below you without stooping. If you bought fixed-length trekking poles in Nairobi, grip lower on the foam extension on the way up and higher on the way down.

Setting up a pole in five steps

  1. Stand on flat ground in the boots you will hike in.
  2. Extend the bottom section to its stop mark first, then set the top section to your length.
  3. Close the locks firmly and lean your weight on the pole to check that it does not slip.
  4. Put your hand up through the strap from below, then bring it down to grip the handle with the strap under your palm.
  5. Tighten the strap so it takes some of your weight without pinching your wrist.

Set up this way, trekking poles in Nairobi or anywhere else let the strap carry part of the load and your grip can stay relaxed for hours, which is what saves your hands and shoulders on a long Kilimanjaro descent.

What to Look for When Buying Trekking Poles in Nairobi

When you buy trekking poles in Nairobi, check five things in your hand: the locks, the length range, the weight, the grip and the tips. The table below gives a quick way to judge any pole before you pay.

One or two? A single pole is fine for balance on a day hike and leaves a hand free for photos. For multi-day treks on Mt Kenya or Kilimanjaro, two poles share the load evenly between both arms and give a steadier rhythm. If you are buying trekking poles in Nairobi for your first climb, start with a pair.

Buying thrifted or pre-owned poles

Second-hand trekking poles in Nairobi can be a very good deal, because a well-made aluminium pole outlasts many boots. Before you buy one, extend every section fully and look along the shaft for bends or dents, especially just above the tip. Open and close each lock several times and lean on it. Check that the carbide tip is not worn flat, that the strap stitching is intact, and that a folding pole's inner cord still pulls the sections snugly together.

Pro Tips for Using Poles

  • Practise close to home: try new trekking poles in Nairobi's Karura Forest before your first big descent.
  • Lengthen before the top: adjust your poles at the summit or rim while you rest, not halfway down a slope.
  • Plant, then step: on steep ground, place the pole first and let it take weight before your boot moves.
  • Stow for scrambles: collapse and strap them to your pack where you need your hands on rock.
  • Mind the group: carry poles tips-down and forward on narrow paths so nobody behind walks into them.
  • Dry them open: after a wet hike, take telescoping poles apart and let each section dry.

How Do You Use Trekking Poles Without Tripping Over Them?

Use trekking poles in a natural rhythm: the left pole lands as the right foot steps, and the right pole with the left foot. Keep the tips behind or beside your front foot on climbs, and slightly ahead of you on descents, so they support you rather than trip you.

On the climb

Short poles and short steps work best uphill. Plant the poles close to your body and push down and back through the straps, so your arms help your legs on long grinds such as the forest section of Ol Donyo Sabuk. On very steep pitches, plant both poles together and step up between them.

On the descent

Going down, lengthen the poles, bend your knees slightly and plant the poles a little ahead before each step. On loose ash or scree, keep your weight over your feet rather than leaning back on the poles, which is what makes boots shoot out from under you. Our Mt Longonot hike guide covers the steepest sections where this technique matters most.

Mistakes that catch out new pole users

The most common mistake is setting poles too long, which pushes your shoulders up and tires your arms in an hour. The second is gripping hard without using the straps. The third is trusting a lock that was never fully closed. Lean on each pole at the trailhead; it takes five seconds. Finally, do not rely on poles to replace good boots: they add balance, not grip. Getting these basics right matters more than which trekking poles in Nairobi you choose.

Looking after poles between hikes

  1. Knock off mud and wipe the shafts with a damp cloth after each hike.
  2. Take telescoping poles apart and let every section dry fully before storing, so the joints do not corrode.
  3. Store them unlocked and loosely collapsed, which takes strain off twist-lock expanders.
  4. Check lever-lock tension now and then and tighten the small screw if the pole slips.
  5. Replace worn rubber covers and baskets; they are cheap and easy to swap.

Looked after like this, a sturdy pair of trekking poles in Nairobi's dust and rain should last for many seasons of hiking.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do beginners actually need trekking poles?

Beginners do not need trekking poles for a first gentle hike, but many find them helpful sooner than expected. New hikers often have the least practice on steep, loose descents, which is exactly where poles add balance and spare the knees. If your first hikes include Mt Longonot or Ol Donyo Sabuk, a single folding pole is a sensible, low-cost first step.

Is one trekking pole enough, or should I get two?

One trekking pole is enough for balance on most day hikes near Nairobi and leaves a hand free. Two poles are better for long descents, multi-day treks and carrying a heavy pack, because they spread the effort across both arms and keep your body square. If you are buying trekking poles in Nairobi for Mt Kenya or Kilimanjaro, plan on a pair and practise with both.

Can I carry trekking poles in my hand luggage?

Trekking poles usually cannot go in hand luggage, because airport security in many countries treats them as items that could be used as a weapon. Pack them in your checked bag, collapsed and with tip covers on, when flying to Kilimanjaro or elsewhere. Rules vary by airport and airline, so confirm with your airline before you fly.

The price of trekking poles in Nairobi depends on the design, materials and whether they are new or pre-owned. Thrifted poles from good brands can offer real savings, provided the locks and shafts are in sound condition.

Are trekking poles allowed in Kenyan national parks?

Trekking poles are widely used on hiking trails in Kenyan national parks such as Mt Longonot, Mt Kenya and the Aberdares, and guides often recommend them. Fitting rubber tip covers on worn or rocky paths reduces trail damage and noise. Park rules can change, so confirm any current requirements with Kenya Wildlife Service or Kenya Forest Service before your hike.

Final Thoughts

Knees remember every descent, and a pole is the cheapest way to make them forgive you. Pick a design that packs small, set it to suit your height, and lengthen it before you start down. Chosen this way, trekking poles in Nairobi pay for themselves on the first loose slope of the short rains.
